items.content:
ERP in manufacturing is more than a back-office system.

It becomes powerful when it connects planning, inventory, procurement, execution, cost, and supply chain visibility in one flow.

Without ERP discipline, teams often face wrong production priorities, inaccurate stock, delayed purchasing, manual updates, poor cost visibility, and disconnected departments.

Here’s how ERP supports manufacturing:

→ 𝗣𝗿𝗼𝗱𝘂𝗰𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝗣𝗹𝗮𝗻𝗻𝗶𝗻𝗴
Create realistic schedules by balancing materials, labor, and capacity.

Start by reviewing open orders and identifying immediate production priorities.

→ 𝗜𝗻𝘃𝗲𝗻𝘁𝗼𝗿𝘆 𝗠𝗮𝗻𝗮𝗴𝗲𝗺𝗲𝗻𝘁
Track materials accurately across warehouses and production.

Start by identifying fast-moving, slow-moving, and critical inventory items.

→ 𝗣𝗿𝗼𝗰𝘂𝗿𝗲𝗺𝗲𝗻𝘁 𝗠𝗮𝗻𝗮𝗴𝗲𝗺𝗲𝗻𝘁
Manage purchasing from supplier selection to delivery.

Start by standardizing supplier records and approved vendor information.

→ 𝗠𝗮𝗻𝘂𝗳𝗮𝗰𝘁𝘂𝗿𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗘𝘅𝗲𝗰𝘂𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻
Track production orders from release to completion.

Start by connecting work orders with routing and resources.

→ 𝗖𝗼𝘀𝘁 & 𝗙𝗶𝗻𝗮𝗻𝗰𝗶𝗮𝗹 𝗖𝗼𝗻𝘁𝗿𝗼𝗹
Understand product costs and manufacturing profitability.

Start by breaking costs into material, labor, and overhead.

→ 𝗦𝘂𝗽𝗽𝗹𝘆 𝗖𝗵𝗮𝗶𝗻 𝗩𝗶𝘀𝗶𝗯𝗶𝗹𝗶𝘁𝘆
Connect suppliers, inventory, production, and customer demand.

Start by mapping critical supply chain dependencies and bottlenecks.

The common mistake?

Using ERP as a record-keeping system instead of an operational control system.

The real value comes when ERP data reflects what is actually happening on the shop floor.

Save this if you work with ERP, manufacturing, supply chain, production planning, or operations.

Stop asking AI to write LinkedIn posts.

Do this instead:

Step 1: Sign up for Stanley.
Step 2: Complete the onboarding.
Step 3: Follow the process below.

Try it (14-days free) → https://lnkd.in/eDh9YRNc

Stanley drafts in your voice by reading your posts. 

Bonus: Repost ♻️ this + DM me the word "Stanley".
I'll send the 4-min walkthrough and 9 more prompts.

1. Mine your voice before you write

✦ Paste your 10 best posts
✦ Ask for tone and themes
✦ Save the profile. Reuse it forever.

"Pull my last 10 posts. Map my sentence patterns and recurring themes. Save it as a voice profile I can reuse."

Generic AI averages everyone. Specifics are the moat.

2. Stock a content bank

✦ List 5 recent wins or hot takes
✦ Tag each with lesson, emotion, angles
✦ File by reader pain point

"Here are 5 moments from my work this month. For each, pull out the lesson, the emotion, and 3 angles to write from."

Real names and exact numbers AI cannot copy.

3. Generate hooks, not posts

✦ Ask for 10 hook variations
✦ Cut anything over 12 words
✦ Pick the one with a number in it

"Write me 10 scroll-stopping hooks for [topic]. Under 10 words each. Specific and curiosity-led."

Aim for 6 to 7 words. Short beats clever.

4. Map the structure

✦ Pick the winning hook
✦ Outline before you write
✦ 3 key beats. No more.

"Outline a post for [idea]. Hook, 3 beats, transition, closing line that drives action. Nothing else."

Re-hook on line 2 to force the "see more" click.

5. Stack your proof points

✦ Claim in one line
✦ One stat, one story, one contrarian take
✦ Cut anything you cannot source

"I want to make this point: [X]. Back it with one stat, one story from my own work, and one contrarian angle."

Disagree with the obvious. Tension stops the scroll.

6. Reformat for the feed

✦ Sentences under 55 characters
✦ Blank line between each beat
✦ First 2 lines carry the whole post

"Reformat this draft for LinkedIn. Break lines. Cut filler. Make it scannable in 20 seconds."

White space chunks ideas into bite-sized beats.

7. Strip the AI tells

✦ Cut clichés and rhetorical questions
✦ Kill em dashes and filler words
✦ Active voice. Zero adverbs.

"Scan this for AI giveaways. Kill rhetorical questions. Cut robotic phrasing. Rewrite any cliché in my voice."

Read it aloud. If it trips your tongue, it trips their eyes.

8. Lock it into a system

✦ Save the full prompt chain
✦ Build a reusable skill
✦ Run it for every new post

"Turn this whole chain into a custom prompt template. One input. Eight outputs. Reusable for every post."

One template kills 80% of blank-page dread.

Most people type "write me a post about X."
Then wonder why it sounds like everyone else.

items.content:
Here is a highly concise, executive summary of the Supply Chain Metrics cheat sheet. It condenses the 14 key performance indicators into 4 core operational pillars for fast, high-level review.
1. Demand & Capacity Planning
Forecast Accuracy: Measures variance between forecasted and actual demand to reduce planning variability.
Capacity Utilization: Tracks actual vs. maximum possible production output to balance underutilization against operational overload.
2. Sourcing, Inventory & Cost Efficiency
Inventory Turnover & Days of Inventory (DOI): Dual metrics tracking asset efficiency-how fast stock sells versus how many days of supply are tied up in inventory.
Total Landing Cost: Captures the true, fully burdened cost of an item (Price + Freight + Duties + Handling).
Cash-to-Cash Cycle Time: Measures total days cash is frozen between paying suppliers (DPO) and collecting revenue (DSO), influenced by inventory velocity (DIO).
3. Warehouse & Logistics Speed
Dock-to-Stock Cycle Time: Measures the internal throughput speed from receiving goods to warehouse stock availability.
Order-to-Delivery Lead Time: Tracks total elapsed time from the initial customer order date to the final physical delivery date.
Supply Chain Cycle Time: An end-to-end macro metric covering the entire SCOR model workflow: $\text{Plan} (rightarrow \text{Source} \rightarrow |text{Make} \rightarrow |text{Deliver} \rightarrow \text{Return}$.
4. Customer Fulfillment & Service Level
Perfect Order Rate: The ultimate reliability standard-orders delivered on time, complete, damage-free, and accurately documented.
On-Time In-Full (OTIF): Measures the baseline execution performance of delivery punctuality and completeness.
Fill Rate vs. Backorder Rate: Inverse indicators tracking immediate product availability from stock versus the percentage of demand delayed due to stockouts.

items.content:
A CEO told me last month that his supply chain team is running flat out and falling further behind every quarter.

I asked him what tools they were using. MRP. Forecast-driven. Same system they installed in 1998 getting ready for the Y2K crisis.

I asked him what had changed since 1998. 

He laughed. 

EVERYTHING. 

Customer expectations. 
Product complexity. 
Lead time pressure. 
Supplier reliability. 
Demand volatility. 
Geopolitics.  

The only thing that didn't change is now it is a real crisis. 

Everything changed. The planning tools did not.

MRP was designed in the 1960s for a stable world with predictable demand and reliable supply. That world is gone. It has been gone for a long time. And the planning profession has been absorbing the consequences every single day.

Your planners are not failing. Their tools are failing them.

I know because I have been on that shop floor. I started at minimum wage. I have run the plant. I have sweated payroll. And I have stared at a screen full of exception messages knowing that the system is telling me to do things that will make the problem worse.

The answer is not a better forecast. The answer is not a fancier algorithm. The answer is not AI layered on top of broken logic.

The answer is to stop pushing product based on predictions and start pulling based on what is actually happening.  Successful companies sense and adapt to the world around them.  Agility with stability.  But how?

Strategically placed decoupling points. Buffers that adjust dynamically. Execution visibility your planners can trust without building a shadow system in Excel.

Roughly right is better than precisely wrong.

The methodology exists. It works in pharma, automotive, chemicals, consumer goods, aerospace. Across six continents. In companies with 50 employees and companies with 50,000.

The only barrier is the deep belief that "this is just how supply chain is."

It is not. I have spent 50 years proving it is not.

What planning assumption is your company still running on that everybody knows is wrong but nobody will say out loud?

items.content:
Like many people, I’ve been trying to get my head around AI in procurement. A post by Asmaa Gad this week really helped. Her Agentic AI Platforms Map (65 platforms, 10 categories, 2026 edition) brilliantly illustrates how crowded this space has become.

Given the number of platforms and categories, I wanted to step back and understand what they actually do. The discussion that followed provided the answer. AI platforms can broadly be viewed as operating across three layers:
- Orchestration: automating end-to-end procurement workflows (e.g. major Source-to-Pay suites such as Coupa, SAP Ariba, GEP)
- Domain Intelligence: generating insight within specific areas—spend analytics (Sievo, Rosslyn), contract intelligence (Icertis, Ironclad), supplier risk (Resilinc, Prewave)
- Data Access: the foundational layer—connectivity, supplier data, and infrastructure that everything else depends on (Palantir, E2open, One Network)

It’s worth noting that the major S2P platforms are increasingly bundling spend analytics and risk monitoring into their core offerings. So are these truly three distinct categories, or three overlapping capabilities? Perhaps the more useful question isn’t “which platform category do I need?” but “which capability will deliver the greatest improvement in performance?” For most teams, it’s the intelligence layer. The workflows already exist—genuinely understanding what you’re spending, with whom, and at what risk is where AI could close the gap first.

items.content:
Deloitte published a piece on the agentic supply chain worth reading if you’re in manufacturing or supply chain.

A few things that stood out:
• Agents support a more continuous planning approach through sensing, decision-making, and response instead of waiting on traditional planning cycles.
• This isn’t one agent doing everything. It’s layered across cross-functional, domain, and task-level agents working together across the flow.
• Dropping agents into existing workflows may miss the mark. Redesigning workflows around what humans and agents each do well provides more benefit.
• Humans still own oversight, judgment, and decision thresholds. Agents operate within those boundaries. Governance is treated as foundational, not something added later.

Deloitte also cited Gartner’s projection that ~50% of supply chain management solutions will include agentic AI by 2030. I can see this happening.

Lately I’ve been using Claude to run some simple agents with anonymized data. Things like checking planning data (lead times, purchase order dates, safety stock, etc.), flagging errors, and suggesting corrections based on defined rules or analysis. I’ve also been using it to run existing Python scripts against historical demand and generate forecast recommendations across different models for comparison and approval.

It’s still early, though the shift is noticeable from a productivity standpoint.

Curious how much value is showing up in practice for others?

#SupplyChain #AI

If you want true inbound from LinkedIn: EVERY SINGLE post needs a JOB. This four-bucket funnel is how I build six-figure pipelines from content.

Most people post whatever comes to mind and hope for the best.

That's a slot machine, not a strategy.

After building some of the biggest personal brands on LinkedIn (and growing my own agency to $1M+ in revenue from content alone), I realized every post falls into one of four buckets.

Each one has a specific job in the funnel:

→ Growth (40% of posts)
Gets you discovered by new people.
Hot takes, industry commentary, bold observations.
This is your top of funnel. Broad enough to attract, sharp enough to stand out.

→ Authority (30% of posts)
Makes them trust you.
Frameworks, systems, case studies, client results.
This is where you prove you can actually deliver.

→ Conversion (20% of posts)
Turns followers into clients.
Direct offers, lead magnets, clear CTAs.
This is where content becomes revenue.

→ Personal (10% of posts)
Makes them remember YOU.
Stories, behind the scenes, real moments.
People buy from people they feel connected to.

Each type feeds the next.

Growth posts bring new eyes → Authority posts build trust → Conversion posts drive action → Personal posts keep them engaged.

That's a flywheel, not just a content calendar.

I used this exact system to bring in 500+ emails, 20+ leads, 3 recurring high-ticket deals closed, 2 consulting deals, and get booked and paid to speak in China. With zero outbound messages in March.

Save this. Screenshot it. Build your next month of content around it.

Your content should be working as hard as you do.
